source_refs.note: Chapter 1 exercise (PDF 19-21), solved: 12 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key is printed), 13 short-answer and 4 descriptive questions with model answers. MCQ VII, Short (e) and (h) and the chapter's Na/Mg equations carry Book corrections.

blocks.text: Q.1 Four choices are given for each question. Select the correct choice.

blocks.prompt: I. Which scientist first time observed the periodicity in the elements?
blocks.explanation: The chapter (1.1): in 1864 John Newlands first time observed periodicity in the 62 known elements; every eighth element resembled the first (arranged by atomic mass). Döbereiner (1829) made triads, and Mendeleev (1869) and Meyer came later.

blocks.prompt: II. Recognize the element if it has 3 electron shells, belongs to “s” block and has 2 electrons in its outer most shell.
blocks.explanation: 3 shells means period 3; s block with 2 valence electrons means group 2. So the element is magnesium, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² (1.6). Calcium has 4 shells; sodium has 1 outer electron.

blocks.prompt: III. Which one do you think is correct about metallic character?

options.text: It decreases from top to bottom in a group.
It increases from top to bottom in a group.
It remains constant from left to right in a period.
It increases from left to right in a period.

blocks.explanation: Down a group atomic size and shielding increase, so valence electrons are lost more easily: metallic character increases (Cs is more metallic than Na). Across a period it decreases (1.7.8).

blocks.prompt: IV. Which one is the correct statement among the following?

options.text: Anionic radius is generally smaller than atomic radius.
Cationic radius is generally bigger than atomic radius.
Cationic ionic radius is generally smaller than atomic radius.
Both anionic and cationic radii are smaller than atomic radius.

blocks.explanation: A cation is smaller than its atom (losing electrons reduces repulsion and the rest are pulled closer); an anion is larger than its atom (1.7.2), e.g. Na 186 pm, Na⁺ 95 pm; Cl 99 pm, Cl⁻ 181 pm.

blocks.prompt: V. Which property increases as you go down a group in the periodic table?
blocks.explanation: Down a group new shells are added, so the atomic radius increases; electron affinity, electronegativity and ionization energy decrease (1.7.1, 1.7.3-1.7.7).

blocks.prompt: VI. Which set of the following conditions results in higher ionization energy?

options.text: Smaller atom and greater nuclear charge.
Smaller atom and smaller nuclear charge
larger atom and greater nuclear charge
larger atom and the smaller nuclear charge

blocks.explanation: Ionization energy increases with greater (effective) nuclear charge and decreases with size; so a small atom with a large nuclear charge holds its electrons most strongly (1.7.3).

blocks.prompt: VII. Which of the following atoms show more than one (variable) oxidation states?
blocks.explanation: Phosphorus shows +3 (P₄O₆, PCl₃) and +5 (P₄O₁₀, PCl₅) because it can expand its octet using empty 3d orbitals; Na (+1), Mg (+2) and Al (+3) each show one oxidation state (1.10).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (d) is printed “Phosphorous”; the element is spelled phosphorus (“phosphorous” is an adjective). The same spelling appears in Short Q (h).

blocks.prompt: VIII. Which is the correct general trend in the variation of electron affinity in a group?

options.text: It becomes less negative from top to bottom.
It becomes more negative from top to bottom.
It has no definite trend and changes irregularly.

blocks.explanation: Down a group the atom grows, the incoming electron is attracted less, so less energy is released: electron affinity becomes less negative (Li −60 to Cs −46 kJ mol⁻¹), with fluorine as an exception (1.7.5).

blocks.prompt: IX. What is the oxidation state of sulfur in the sulfate ion (SO₄²⁻).
X. Which is the correct trend in variation of electronegativity along a period of the periodic table?

options.text: It decreases from left to right across a period.
It increases from left to right across a period.

blocks.explanation: Across a period nuclear charge increases and size decreases, so electronegativity increases (Li 1.0 to F 4.0) (1.7.7).

blocks.prompt: XI. The atomic radius generally…….. across a period in the periodic table.
blocks.explanation: Across a period the number of shells stays the same while nuclear charge increases and pulls the electron cloud closer, so the atomic radius decreases (1.7.1).

blocks.prompt: XII. Which one of the following elements has the highest ionization energy?
blocks.explanation: All four are in period 3. Argon, a noble gas with a completely filled 3s² 3p⁶ shell, has the highest ionization energy in its period (1.7.3).

blocks.text: Q.2 Attempt the following short-answer questions:

blocks.prompt: a. What is 1st ionization energy? Give an example.
blocks.explanation:
The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions (ΔHᵢ₁).
Example: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔHᵢ₁ = 494 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.prompt: b. Explain why sulfur has a lower first ionization energy than phosphorus.
blocks.explanation: P (3s² 3p³) has a stable half-filled 3p subshell, so removing an electron is difficult. In S (3s² 3p⁴) one 3p orbital holds a spin-paired electron pair; their repulsion makes one of them easier to remove. So IE of S < IE of P.

blocks.prompt: c. Why the elements in Group 13 to 17 are called p-block elements?
blocks.explanation: Because their valence (last) electrons enter p orbitals; their valence shell configuration is ns² np¹ to ns² np⁵ (group 18, ns² np⁶, is also p block).

blocks.prompt: d. What are the factors that affect electronegativity?
blocks.explanation:
1. Atomic size: larger atom, lower electronegativity (F > Cl > Br > I).
2. Effective nuclear charge: greater charge, greater electronegativity; so it increases across a period (Li 1.0, F 4.0).

blocks.prompt: e. What factors are responsible for the the increasing reactivity of alkali metals as you move down the group?
blocks.explanation: Down the group: atomic size increases and the shielding effect of inner shells increases, so the single valence electron is held less tightly; ionization energy decreases (Li > Na > K > Rb > Cs) and the electron is lost more easily, so reactivity increases.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question is printed with a doubled word: “for the the increasing reactivity”.

blocks.prompt: f. Why some of the elements show variable oxidation numbers while others do not?
blocks.explanation: Oxidation number equals the number of electrons used in bonding. Elements such as P and S have empty 3d orbitals and can excite paired electrons into them (expand the octet), so they can use different numbers of electrons (P: +3, +5; S: +4, +6). Na, Mg, Al have no such choice and use all valence electrons (+1, +2, +3).

blocks.prompt: g. Identify the element which is in period 5 and group 15?
blocks.explanation: Antimony (Sb, Z = 51): 5 shells, valence configuration 5s² 5p³ (5 valence electrons, p block).

blocks.prompt: h. Why oxides of sodium and magnesium are more ionic than the oxides of nitrogen and phosphorous?
blocks.explanation: Na and Mg are metals with low electronegativity (0.9, 1.2); the electronegativity difference with O (3.5) is large, so electrons are transferred and giant ionic lattices form (Na₂O, MgO). N (3.0) and P (2.1) are non-metals with small differences, so they share electrons and form covalent molecular oxides.

blocks.prompt: i. Give reason for the different chemical reactivities of Na and Mg toward oxygen and chlorine.
blocks.explanation: Na loses only one electron (low IE 494 kJ mol⁻¹) and is larger, so it is more metallic and reacts more vigorously (burns with a golden yellow flame; kept under kerosene). Mg must lose two electrons (higher total IE) and is smaller, so it reacts less readily (needs heating; burns with an intense white flame).

blocks.prompt: j. Why the ionization energy of lithium is much lower than that of helium despite the fact that the nuclear charge of lithium is +3 and that of helium is +2.
blocks.explanation: Li (1s² 2s¹) loses its 2s electron, which is in a new, farther shell and is shielded by the two 1s electrons, so it feels a small effective nuclear charge. He (1s²) loses an electron from a completely filled first shell, close to the nucleus with no shielding. So IE of He (2372) ≫ Li (520 kJ mol⁻¹) (values beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: k. The ionization energy of Be (atomic no. 4) is higher than that of B (atomic no. 5), despite the fact that the nuclear charge of Be is +4 and that of B is +5.
blocks.explanation: Be (1s² 2s²) has a completely filled, stable 2s subshell. In B (1s² 2s² 2p¹) the electron removed is a single 2p electron, which has higher energy than 2s and is shielded by the 2s electrons. So it is removed more easily: IE of B < IE of Be.

blocks.prompt: l. What is common in Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, Ne⁰ and F⁻? Arrange them in increasing order of sizes.
blocks.explanation:
All are isoelectronic: each has 10 electrons, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ (neon configuration).
With the same electrons, more protons pull the cloud in more strongly:
Al³⁺ (13 p) < Mg²⁺ (12 p) < Na⁺ (11 p) < Ne (10 p) < F⁻ (9 p)

blocks.prompt:
m. Consider the chlorides of sodium, magnesium, and phosphorus(V): NaCl, MgCl₂, and PCl₅
(i) Classify each of these chlorides as acidic, basic, or neutral.
(ii) For each chloride, briefly explain the reason for your classification, referring to their behavior when dissolved in water.
blocks.explanation:
(i) NaCl: neutral; MgCl₂: neutral (very slightly acidic, pH 6.5); PCl₅: acidic. None is basic.
(ii) NaCl and MgCl₂ are ionic; they only dissolve and hydrate, no hydrolysis:
NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) (pH 7)
MgCl₂(s) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) (pH 6.5)
PCl₅ is covalent; it is hydrolysed by water to acids:
PCl₅ + 4H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 5HCl (pH below 7) (equation beyond the chapter)

blocks.prompt: Q.3 Write equations for the reactions of Na and Mg with oxygen, chlorine, and water. Compare the reactivity of both elements with these in terms of metallic character.
blocks.explanation:
With water:
2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g) (vigorous, cold water)
Mg(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Mg(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g) (slow)
Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g) (with steam, vigorous)
With oxygen:
2Na(s) + O₂(g) → Na₂O₂(s) (in open air; peroxide)
4Na(s) + O₂(g) → 2Na₂O(s) (limited O₂ or high temperature)
2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s) (intense white flame)
With chlorine:
2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s) (exothermic, golden yellow flame)
Mg(s) + Cl₂(g) → MgCl₂(s)
Comparison: Na (group 1) is more metallic than Mg (group 2): it is larger and loses only one electron (lower ionization energy), so it reacts more vigorously with water, oxygen and chlorine. Na reacts violently with cold water and must be kept under kerosene; Mg reacts slowly with cold water and vigorously only with steam, and burns in oxygen only when heated. Both form white ionic solids (NaCl, MgCl₂, MgO) and basic oxides/hydroxides.

rows: Smaller atom, higher total ionization energy
Slow with cold water; vigorous with steam
Burns in air to Na₂O₂ / Na₂O
Burns when heated, intense white flame, MgO

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the chapter (1.8) three of these equations are misprinted: “2Na(s) + O₂(g) → 2Na₂O₂(s)” is not balanced (it is 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂); magnesium oxide is printed as a gas, “2MgO(g)” (it is the white solid 2MgO(s)); and the steam reaction is printed “Mg(s) + 2H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g)”, which is not balanced (it is Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂). The answer above gives the corrected equations.

blocks.prompt: Q.4 Explain with the help of equations acidic and basic behavior of oxides and chlorides.
blocks.explanation:
Oxides:
1. Basic oxides: oxides of metals (groups 1, 2), ionic; with water they give alkalis.
Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq)
CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq)
2. Amphoteric oxide: Al₂O₃ is insoluble in water but reacts with both acids and bases.
Al₂O₃(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O(l)
Al₂O₃(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂Al₂O₄ + H₂O(l)
3. Acidic oxides: oxides of non-metals, covalent; with water they give acids and they react with bases.
P₂O₃(s) + 3H₂O(l) → 2H₃PO₃(aq)
SO₂(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂SO₃(aq)
SiO₂(s) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SiO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
SO₂(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
Across period 3 oxides change from basic (Na₂O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to acidic (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃).
Chlorides:
1. Neutral chlorides: NaCl and MgCl₂ (ionic) only dissolve and hydrate, no hydrolysis.
NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) (pH 7)
MgCl₂(s) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) (pH 6.5)
2. Acidic chlorides: from Al to S the chlorides are hydrolysed by water, giving HCl (pH below 7).
AlCl₃(s) + 3H₂O(l) → Al(OH)₃(s) + 3HCl(aq)
SiCl₄(l) + 2H₂O(l) → SiO₂(s) + 4HCl(aq)
PCl₃(l) + 3H₂O(l) → H₃PO₃ + 3HCl(aq)
The covalent character of chlorides increases across the period as the electronegativity difference with Cl decreases.

blocks.prompt: Q.5 Describe the factors affecting and periodic trends of electron affinity.
blocks.explanation:
Electron affinity (ΔH°ₑₐ₁): the enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous uni-negative ions under standard conditions.
Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)   ΔH°ₑₐ₁ = −348.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (energy released, negative sign)
The second electron affinity is positive (energy absorbed): O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g)   ΔH°ₑₐ₂ = +798 kJ mol⁻¹.
Factors:
1. Size of atom: the smaller the atom, the stronger the nuclear attraction for the incoming electron, the greater the electron affinity.
2. Nuclear charge: greater nuclear charge, greater electron affinity.
3. Electronic configuration: atoms with half-filled subshells (N 2s² 2p³, P 3s² 3p³) have very low electron affinity; noble gases (ns² np⁶) do not accept electrons (positive values).
Periodic trends:
1. Down a group: size increases, attraction for the added electron decreases, so electron affinity generally decreases (becomes less negative), e.g. Li −60, Na −53, K −48, Rb −47, Cs −46 kJ mol⁻¹. In halogens: At < I < Br < F < Cl; fluorine is less than chlorine because its very small size crowds the incoming electron (strong repulsion of its compact 2p electrons) (reason beyond the chapter).
2. Across a period: electron affinity becomes more negative from left to right because nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases; halogens have the highest values in each period.

blocks.prompt: Q.6 Describe the factors affecting and periodic trends of ionization energy.
blocks.explanation:
Ionization energy: the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions (ΔHᵢ₁), e.g. Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔHᵢ₁ = 494 kJ mol⁻¹. Successive ionization energies increase (Ca: 590, 1150, 4940 kJ mol⁻¹).
Factors:
1. Nuclear charge: greater effective nuclear charge, stronger attraction, higher ionization energy.
2. Size of atom: bigger atom, weaker hold on outer electrons, lower ionization energy.
3. Electronic arrangement: half-filled and completely filled subshells are more stable, so ionization energy is higher; noble gases (ns² np⁶) have the highest values; N (half-filled 2p³, 1403 kJ mol⁻¹) is higher than O.
4. Shielding effect: more inner electrons, more screening, lower ionization energy.
5. Spin-pair repulsion: a spin-paired electron (as in O 2p⁴) is slightly easier to remove than an unpaired one (N).
Periodic trends:
1. Down a group: nuclear charge increases, but size and shielding increase more, so ionization energy decreases: Li > Na > K > Rb > Cs.
2. Across a period: shells stay the same while effective nuclear charge increases, so ionization energy generally increases; alkali metals have the lowest and noble gases the highest values in each period. Small dips occur at B (after Be), O (after N), Al (after Mg) and S (after P).
